candidates.title: CASTLE: training natural language search before the first real query
candidates.summary: How we addressed the cold-start problem for Airbnb’s natural language search by jointly generating synthetic training data — queries and relevance labels — from de-identified booking and search signals. By : Wendy Ran Wei , Hao Li , Weiwei Guo , Xiaowei Liu , Xueyin Chen , Chun How Tan , Malay Haldar , Soumyadip Banerjee , Kedar Bellare , Huiji Gao , Sanjeev Katariya , and Stephanie Moyerman Introduction Natural language search lets guests express intent in their own words, such as “romantic cabin near skiing” or “pet-friendly beach house that sleeps eight,” rather than navigating filters and categories. We needed to introduce this kind of search for Airbnb, and to have it work well from the start. However, this required training the model before we had actual user queries to train the model on, and a reasonable set of relevance labels (inferred from the queries) to map queries to matching listings. Without prior traffic, both must be synthesized from scratch. This is the cold-start problem for natural-language search. Other organizations have faced similar challenges and have created methods to address them. However, prior approaches address the need for a body of queries and the need for relevance labels separately. Passage-based methods such as InPars [1] prompt a large language model (LLM) to generate queries conditioned on a single document, then rely on additional LLM judgments to assign relevance labels, introducing a second source of error. candidates.title: Staying close to the craft in a rapidly shifting industry
candidates.summary: What I’ve learned from moving between IC and manager roles and why staying hands-on matters, especially in this new AI-obsessed world Photo by Kelly Boitano It was really only a few years ago when the general concept of “growth” was straightforward for a designer navigating their career path: keep climbing the ladder until you become a manager, then let go of the hands-on work for good — and keep on climbing. That model is breaking down right in front of us. More and more designers are choosing to stay close to the craft; driving impact, leading others, and executing at a high level without ever moving into a traditional management role. But I think we’re already past that being the most interesting shift. With AI tools accelerating what a single designer can build, and with companies rethinking what they need from their teams, the line between making and managing is getting blurrier by the day. The question isn’t “Which track do I pick?” anymore. It’s “What kind of builder do I want to be right now?” I’ve been navigating this question for most of my career, but framed up as “management vs. IC” well before it became a broader industry conversation. I’d like to share what I’ve learned, as one designer’s story of figuring it out in real time. Bouncing between making and managing I’ve bounced around in title a lot. candidates.title: Faire’s agentic development culture
candidates.summary: How we’re working towards our long-term vision of a lights-out codebase In early 2025, it was already clear that the incremental capability of models would be accelerating, eventually crossing a threshold for autonomous code delivery. With each big frontier model launch, more and more engineers were changing their day-to-day execution from autocomplete assistance to prompt engineering. At Faire , we didn’t want to wait for the frontier model vendors to eventually cross the efficacy threshold, or come out with the generic tooling, before we drove adoption. We wanted to squeeze the most out of existing capability, while starting the long-term work of hardening the prerequisites for an agent harness that upgrades capability into reliability . This article describes our adoption journey so far, and the principles behind it. Principles Let’s start with the principles. Over the course of our journey, we’ve developed two key principles that have guided our approach to Faire’s agentic culture so far, and will continue to do so in the future: Just build it. Every engineering org will have the same continuous debate: build or buy. When a new capability emerges, do you wait for a vendor to package it up and sell it to you, or do you build a thin version yourself and start learning today? Our answer has consistently been: just build it! This is not because we think we can out-engineer the frontier labs. We can’t, and don’t try to. The strategy is more disciplined than that. candidates.title: Spec, review, ship: How AI is changing the way Faire builds software
candidates.summary: Highlights from our July 2026 Kitchener-Waterloo Tech Talk Written with Hyma Acharya , Zach Radford , Quinn Budan , and Vaibhav Singh Faire Tech Talk speakers: Vaibhav Singh , Hyma Acharya , Mark Widish , Zach Radford , Quinn Budan . Earlier this month, we welcomed Kitchener-Waterloo’s tech community into our office for a Tech Talk dedicated to how Faire engineers build. Across four talks, our speakers shared how AI is changing the way Faire builds software, from spec-driven development to AI code review and AI testing, all with the goal of delivering real value for the brands and retailers we serve. You can watch a video recording of the event . AI coding tools can move quickly, but they need clear context. Consider this prompt: “Add image paste to the product editor.” This doesn’t explain the user problem, technical constraints, validation plan, or possible risks related to the ask. Without this context, AI must fill in the gaps. This context often already exists but it’s spread across product documents, Slack, Jira, and GitHub. candidates.title: Virtual Packer: How Faire estimates shipping costs at checkout
candidates.summary: Combining multimodal machine learning and live carrier rates to estimate shipping costs before an order is packed Picture a boutique owner in Austin browsing Faire , our online wholesale marketplace. They have filled a cart with brands that match the boutique’s character — candles, ceramic mugs, and a few sets of greeting cards — and they’re about to check out. Before they place the order, one cost is still unknown: shipping — and it comes straight off their margin. How much will it cost to ship? It’s an easy question to ask and a deceptively hard one to answer. At the moment of checkout, we don’t yet know — brands ship directly to retailers from their own warehouses. We don’t know which carrier the brand will use, whether they’ll ship ground or overnight, or how they’ll pack the order. The real cost won’t be known for days. Yet the retailer needs a number they can trust right now, since it factors directly into whether the order is worth placing at all. For a long time, our Applied Science team answered with a natural starting point: a model built on each brand’s past shipping behavior. It was fast and stable, but wrong often enough to matter. So we started from a different question. Rather than look up what similar orders cost in the past, we simulate the order as a physical shipment, predicting what it will weigh and how many packages it will need, then price those virtual packages using live carrier rates. candidates.title: Autoscience: How we built agent-driven ML exploration at Faire
candidates.summary: Faire is an online wholesale marketplace connecting independent retailers with brands worldwide. Many of those connections are made possible with machine learning: ranking which products a retailer sees first, deciding which ads are relevant, improving listing quality , and estimating shipping costs. The models underlying these activities share a common problem: there are far more things worth trying (features, architectures, hyperparameters) than any team can reasonably explore. Each iteration demands attention: deciding what to try, reviewing results, and deciding what’s next. Teams end up running a fraction of the ML experiments the problem warrants to be truly optimized. Andrej Karpathy’s Autoresearch offered a promising approach: an agent that iterates on improving a model by proposing a change, training, scoring, keeping the change or reverting, and repeating far more times than a team could in the same span of weeks. However, applying that pattern directly to Faire’s ML systems surfaced practical challenges. To address this, we built Autoscience, named after our AI Applied Science team, to turn agent-driven ML exploration from a promising prototype into a production system used across teams.
